title: Annotatio IV §.X: Mejerus — six ages; sixth accelerates errors and superstitions
pass_a_gloss: And thus far we have known the State of the Christian Religion in the Vth Age indeed good, better in the fourth Age, best in the three first ages; now at last follow the ages in which Christianity begins to rush into the worse, and puts on an altogether new face. This worse State of the Christian Religion, which takes its start in the VIth Age, was in the first times bad, in the middle worse, but in the last, before the reformation, worst. And so from the beginnings of Christ’s Church all the way to the Reformation, we mark in history six distinct intervals, or ages of the Christian religion. In the first five ages we observe new errors and superstitions in the Christian religion swelling gradually and sometimes without sense; finally in the sixth age, by a swifter course and openly, rushing. Although indeed, Mejerus observing, in the sixth Age new errors and superstitions began to rush in and press in by a certain swifter course,
pass_b_english: Mejerus: Age V still good; IV better; the first three best — then ages follow in which Christianity puts on a new, worse face.
Six ages from the Church’s beginnings to the Reformation: errors creep in the first five; in the sixth they rush in faster and openly.
source_text: Et hactenus Statum Religionis Christianæ Seculo quidem V. bonum, meliorem Seculo quarto, optimum tribus primis seculis, cognovimus, nunc demum subsequuntur secula, quibus in deterius ruere incipit Christianismus, atque novam prorsus induit faciem. Deterior hic Religionis Christianæ Status, qui Seculo VI. capit, primis temporibus fuit malus, mediis pejor, ultimis vero, ante reformationem, pessimus. Atque sic à primordiis Ecclesiæ Christi usque ad Reformationem, sex distincta intervalla, seu ætates religionis christianæ, in historia annotamus. Primis quinque seculis sensim & nonnunquam sine sensu gliscere, seculo denique sexto, cursu quodam velociore atque palam ruere in Christianâ religione novos errores ac superstitiones observamus.
